candidate_sources.title: Guignardia Leaf Blotch : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: UMass Extension landscape fact sheet dedicated to Guignardia leaf blotch, describing symptoms (leaf spots and blotches), the causal Guignardia fungus, and management on broad-leaved evergreens including rhododendron and azalea.

candidate_sources.title: Phyllosticta Leaf Blotch : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Phyllosticta species (anamorph/asexual stage of Guignardia) are opportunistic pathogens that cause leaf spots, blotches, marginal leaf blight, and total collapse of infected foliage. The most common hosts of Phyllosticta leaf blotch on broad-leaved evergreens in southern New England include rhododendron/azalea (Rhododendron).

candidate_sources.title: Guignardia Leaf Spot | Plant Disease Diagnostics Clinic - University of Wisconsin-Madison
candidate_sources.snippet: Guignardia leaf spot is caused by the fungus Guignardia (Phyllosticta) which survives in leaf litter. Symptoms include roughly circular or angular, ¼ to ½ inch dead spots, often with a purple-red border and centers that may fall out; young leaves are more susceptible. Management includes sanitation, improved airflow, base watering, and fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper, mancozeb, thiophanate-methyl).

candidate_sources.title: Guignardia Leaf Spot – Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Wisconsin Horticulture extension article on Guignardia leaf spot covering the causal fungus, circular/angular dead spots with reddish-purple borders, disease cycle (overwinters in leaf litter), and management through sanitation, cultural practices, and labeled fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: Exobasidium Gall of Rhododendron and Azalea : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Exobasidium vaccinii is a fungus that causes galls on ericaceous plant species. The first symptoms are swollen or puffy portions on newly expanding leaves, shoots, buds or flowers, which turn into galls that range in color from green, silvery white, to pink or red. As galls age, they develop a white surface growth consisting of reproductive spores; eventually the infected part turns brown and shrivels into hard galls. Fungicide sprays are not effective; prevention involves hand picking the galls off before they develop white sporulating surfaces.

candidate_sources.title: Exobasidium Gall on Azalea | University of Maryland Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Exobasidium gall on azalea is caused by the fungus Exobasidium vaccinii. This problem is more common during cool and wet spring weather. Infection is dependent on high humidity and moisture during bud break. While very noticeable, Exobasidium leaf and flower gall will not threaten the health of the plant. Management involves hand picking galls before they develop white sporulating surfaces and avoiding overhead watering in spring.

candidate_sources.title: Leaf and Flower Gall / Home and Landscape / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaf and flower gall on azalea and camellia is caused by Exobasidium fungi. Infected leaves, buds, and flowers become thickened, curled, fleshy, and pale green to white or pinkish galls. A whitish layer of spores forms on the gall surface. Management focuses on removing and disposing of galls before the white spore layer develops.

candidate_sources.title: Azalea (Rhododendron spp.)-Leaf and Flower Gall | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Azalea (Rhododendron spp.)-Leaf and Flower Gall caused by Exobasidium vaccinii. Symptoms include thickened, curled, fleshy, and distorted leaves and flower parts that are pale green, white, or pink. Galls become covered with a white powdery layer of spores. Cultural and chemical management options are listed.

candidate_sources.title: Azalea Leaf and Flower Gall (FSA-7546) | University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Azalea leaf and flower gall is caused by the fungus Exobasidium vaccinii. The fungus causes abnormal swelling and distortion of leaves and flowers, which become thickened and fleshy. Galls develop a white coating of spores before turning brown. Includes symptoms, disease cycle, and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Rhododendron-Gray Blight | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Pestalotiopsis sydowiana causes gray blight on rhododendrons. The spot is at first white in the middle with a dark-brown margin; later it becomes a blotch, with small fungal fruiting bodies (acervuli) dotting the spot's surface. Leaf infection usually follows an injury such as sunburn, sunscald, or low temperature. Management: choose a planting site to reduce injury, do not take cuttings from infected plants, use a clean sharp tool.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Leaf Spot on Rhododendron delavayi Caused by Pestalotiopsis scoparia in China | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: The damaged leaves show gray-white irregular diseased spots with black-brown margins and black conidiomata on the surface, and when severe, leaves fall. Leaf spot disease is a serious problem for rhododendrons, reducing their ornamental value and causing significant economic losses. First report of Pestalotiopsis scoparia causing leaf spot on Rhododendron delavayi.

candidate_sources.title: Pestalotiopsis kenyana causes leaf spot disease on Rhododendron agastum in China - ScienceDirect
candidate_sources.snippet: Pestalotiopsis kenyana was identified as a pathogen causing leaf spot in Rhododendron agastum, marking the first report of P. kenyana causing leaf spot in this rhododendron species. Damaged leaves show gray-white irregular spots with black-brown margins and black conidiomata.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Azalea Petal Blight Caused by Pestalotiopsis guepini in Argentina | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Pestalotiopsis guepini was reported as the cause of petal blight on azalea flowers in Argentina. Describes symptoms on azalea (Rhododendron spp.) caused by a Pestalotiopsis species.
